extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students, coaches/organizers, and others interested in the Putnam Competition
extracted.subtask_description: Description of the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition: eligibility, schedule, problem scope, scoring, team rules, awards, and participation limits for the annual undergraduate mathematics contest in North America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility (who may participate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual mathematics competition for undergraduate college students enrolled at institutions of higher learning in the United States, Canada, and Mexico (regardless of the students' nationalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At a participating college, any student who wishes to take part in the competition may (limited by the number of spots a school receives); note a student may not participate in the Putnam Competition more than four times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition schedule and sittings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Putnam competition takes place on the first Saturday in December, and consists of two three-hour sittings separated by a lunch break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each sitting is supervised by faculty members at the participating schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem set size and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The competition consists of twelve challenging problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems are arranged across the two sessions (traditionally six per session).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem content scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The problems cover a range of advanced material in undergraduate mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of topics include concepts from group theory, set theory, graph theory, lattice theory, and number theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-problem scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the twelve questions is worth 10 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most frequent scores above zero are 10 points for a complete solution, 9 points for a nearly complete solution, and 1 point for the beginnings of a solution. (In earlier years the twelve questions were worth one point each, with no partial credit given.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall difficulty and expected scores
rubrics_metrics.description: The competition is considered to be very difficult: the median score is often zero or one (out of 120).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of difficulty, high scores are rare (there had been only five perfect scores as of 2021); historical statistics (percent scoring ≥10, cutoffs for top percentiles) are often cited to illustrate difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team composition and ranking rules (pre-2019)
rubrics_metrics.description: Until 2019 the school's official team consisted of three individuals whom it designated in advance, and a team's score was the sum of the ranks of its three team members, with the lowest cumulative rank winning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It was possible for students not on the official team to outscore an official team member, producing counterintuitive team results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team composition and ranking rules (post-2019)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2019 a school's team consists of its top three scorers, and team ranks are determined by comparing the sums of the scores of the team members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change ensures the top performers from a school constitute its team and that teams are ranked by sum of scores rather than summed ranks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Putnam Fellows naming and ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: The top five (or six, in case of a tie) scorers in the competition have been named Putnam Fellows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the top five, Putnam Fellows are not ranked; the top five individual scorers are named Putnam Fellows and (separately) awarded monetary prizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation limit per student
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are not allowed to participate in the Putnam Competition more than four times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a high school senior who officially participates forfeits one year of college eligibility; historically very few have been Putnam Fellows four times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and prize structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary awards are given to top teams and top individuals, and other recognitions are published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The top five teams win $25,000, $20,000, $15,000, $10,000, and $5,000, with team members receiving $1,000, $800, $600, $400, and $200 respectively. The top five individual scorers (Putnam Fellows) are awarded $2,500. Sixth through 15th place individuals receive $1,000 and the next ten receive $250. One of the top five individuals may receive a Putnam Fellow Prize Fellowship (scholarship up to $12,000 plus tuition at Harvard). The names of the top 100 students are published in the American Mathematical Monthly, and names/addresses of the top 500 contestants are mailed to participating institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and announcement timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition results are published in early April of the year following the competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MAA announces winners and publishes a score-to-rank correspondence; archives and problem sets are made available after the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elizabeth Lowell Putnam Award (female high scorer award)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1992, the Elizabeth Lowell Putnam Award has been available to be awarded to a female participant with a high score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three awards were made for the first time in 2019; list of winners and years is maintained.
